contentMarkdown:
Every iPhone records in MOV, and every iPhone user eventually hits the same wall: the clip plays perfectly on your phone but won't open on a Windows PC, an Android phone, a smart TV, or inside some video editors. To convert MOV to MP4 free, you don't need to buy software or install anything — the fastest route runs entirely in your browser, and there are solid offline options for big files too.

## Which method should you pick?

| Method | Best for | Install? | Speed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Browser converter (Method 1) | One clip, any device, no upload | No | Seconds for a remux; minutes for HEVC re-encode |
| VLC (Method 2) | Big files, offline, several clips at once | Yes, free | Depends on your CPU |
| iPhone / Android (Method 3) | Converting on the phone itself | No | Same as the browser converter |
| iMovie on Mac (Method 4) | Mac users who already have iMovie | No — preinstalled | Minutes |

## Method 1: Free MOV to MP4 converter (browser, no upload)

The fastest route is the [free MOV to MP4 converter](/tools/mov-to-mp4-converter), which converts entirely inside your browser with ffmpeg:

1. Open the converter and drop in your `.mov` file (up to about 50 MB).
2. The first visit loads the video engine (~30 MB) once — after that, conversions run locally.
3. Press "Convert to MP4". The tool first tries an instant lossless remux — just repackaging your existing streams into an MP4 container without touching the data.
4. If your MOV needs it (like iPhone HEVC clips, which don't fit every MP4 use case), it re-encodes to H.264 + AAC instead. The result tells you which path it took.
5. Preview the MP4 right on the page, then download it.

The output is a standard MP4 that plays on every phone, TV, and computer — and the H.264 re-encode is typically much smaller than the original MOV, which makes it easier to attach, message, or back up. Your file never leaves your device: no upload, no account, no watermark.

If your clip is in another format — AVI, MKV, WebM — the general [video converter](/tools/video-converter) handles those the same way, in the browser.

## Method 2: VLC (desktop, fully offline)

If you already use VLC media player, it converts MOV to MP4 without any internet connection:

1. Open VLC and choose **Media → Convert / Save**.
2. Add your MOV file and click **Convert / Save**.
3. In the Profile dropdown, choose **Video – H.264 + MP3 (MP4)** (or H.264 + AAC if offered).
4. Set the destination file ending in `.mp4` and click **Start**.

This is the better choice when you're converting on an airplane, on metered data, or when a file sits just over the browser tool's size limit. The same steps work identically on Windows and Mac. You can also add several files to the Convert dialog at once and VLC will work through them one after another.

## Method 3: On your phone

**iPhone:** the browser converter works directly in Safari — choose the MOV from Photos or Files and download the MP4. One setting worth knowing: iPhone's camera can record in a more compatible format. Go to **Settings → Camera → Formats** and choose **Most Compatible** — future recordings save in the more compatible format, so you skip the conversion step entirely. The trade-off is larger file sizes, since HEVC is more efficient.

**Android:** open the converter in Chrome, pick the MOV from your files, and save the MP4 to Downloads. Nothing to install.

## Method 4: iMovie on Mac (no install needed)

If you're on a Mac, iMovie is already installed and exports real MP4 files:

1. Open iMovie and create a new Movie project.
2. Import your MOV clip and drag it onto the timeline.
3. Click **File → Share → File**, pick a resolution, and export.

The exported file is an H.264 MP4 that plays anywhere. It's slower than the browser converter's instant remux, so use it when the file is too big for the browser or you want to trim the clip at the same time.

## Converting several MOV files at once

The browser converter handles one file at a time, so for a batch use VLC or FFmpeg:

- **VLC:** add all your MOVs to the Convert / Save dialog (Method 2 above) and it converts them in sequence.
- **FFmpeg (command line):** one line converts every MOV in a folder — `for f in *.mov; do ffmpeg -i "$f" -c:v libx264 -c:a aac "${f%.mov}.mp4"; done` — and installing FFmpeg is free on Windows, Mac, and Linux.

## Why MP4 plays everywhere and MOV doesn't

MOV is Apple's container format, and it's the codec inside that usually causes the trouble. iPhones record in HEVC (H.265) by default, which some Windows apps, older Android players, and many smart TVs handle badly. The converter's re-encode path produces H.264 + AAC — the one combination essentially every device made in the last decade plays without complaint.

## Fixing common problems

- **The converted MP4 still won't play:** try it in VLC first — if VLC plays it, the file is fine and your other player is the problem. If VLC won't play it either, the source MOV may be corrupted.
- **No audio after converting:** the file probably had an unusual audio codec. The browser converter re-encodes audio to AAC, so run it through Method 1 — if the MOV has no audio track at all, nothing can recover it.
- **Conversion seems stuck:** a lossless remux finishes in seconds, but re-encoding HEVC footage is real video encoding — a long clip on an older phone can take a few minutes. Let it run; if the tab froze, try a smaller file.
- **The MP4 is still too big to send:** run it through the [video compressor](/tools/video-compressor) to shrink it, or pull just the audio out with the [MP4 to MP3 converter](/tools/mp4-to-mp3-converter) if you only need the sound.

## The honest limits

- **File size:** the browser converter caps files at about 50 MB — iPhone video adds up fast (a minute of 4K can be 400 MB), so [trim longer clips first](/tools/video-trimmer) or use the desktop VLC method above for big files.
- **Speed:** a lossless remux is instant; re-encoding HEVC footage takes longer because your device is doing real video encoding. A longer clip on an older phone can take a few minutes.
- **Re-encoded quality:** the HEVC path re-encodes at high quality (CRF 23), which is visually near-lossless, but any re-encode is technically one generation of loss — keep the original MOV if the footage is precious.
- **DRM-protected videos** from streaming services won't convert anywhere — that's by design, not a bug.
